enrichment.short_title: Mabon v Mabon: separate representation of articulate teenagers in residence proceedings

statutes_considered.title: United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989

key_facts: Three boys aged 17, 15 and 13 sought leave under FPR 9.2A(4) to continue residence proceedings without their CAFCAS guardian after a lengthy fact-finding hearing.
Judge Dixon refused the application, citing delay, emotional harm and the view that independent representation would add nothing.
The boys were educated, articulate and assessed by a family practitioner as having sufficient understanding; Dr Gay later confirmed their ability.
Thorpe LJ held the judge plainly wrong and that rule 9.2A(6) mandates leave where sufficient understanding is shown, reflecting children's autonomy under Article 12 UNCRC and Article 8 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of leave under FPR 9.2A(4) to remove the guardian ad litem and represent themselves in the disposal stage of private law residence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; order made under rule 9.2A(4) granting separate representation for each child.
enrichment.ratio: Under FPR 9.2A(6) the court must grant leave to remove a guardian if the child has sufficient understanding to participate without one; for articulate teenagers the right to express views and participate may outweigh paternalistic welfare judgments, though welfare remains relevant where direct participation would pose uncomprehended harm.
legal_issues: Construction of FPR 9.2A(6) and its relationship with Re S (A Minor) (Independent Representation)
Whether the judge wrongly treated welfare as paramount at the leave stage
Whether Article 12 UNCRC and Article 8 ECHR require greater recognition of children's procedural autonomy
Application of the tandem model where guardian and child conflict

Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986] AC 112

notes: State immunity and open justice; full Court of Appeal judgment on confidentiality orders.

enrichment.short_title: Harb v King Fahd: open justice and state immunity in section 27 maintenance proceedings
key_facts: Janan George Harb issued a section 27 application against King Fahd Bin Abdul Aziz alleging failure to provide reasonable maintenance.
The President heard the state immunity preliminary issue in private as Maple v Maple and imposed stringent reporting restrictions.
The Court of Appeal refused the King's application for a private appeal and held the President misdirected herself by eliding the immunity issue with ancillary relief confidentiality.
Thorpe LJ held a claim to state immunity is essentially a public legal issue demanding open litigation, not secret chambers proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against the President's refusal of an open hearing on state immunity and against confidentiality orders made in section 27 proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeals allowed; reporting restrictions in paragraphs 4-6 of the 15 December order deleted and proceedings restored to their true title.
enrichment.ratio: A preliminary issue of state immunity involves only agreed facts and legal argument and should be heard in open court; it cannot be treated like ancillary relief merely because the underlying claim would otherwise be private, and Article 29 Vienna Convention does not require a public appeal hearing to be conducted in private.
legal_issues: Whether the state immunity preliminary issue should have been heard in open court
Whether the President correctly exercised discretion to maintain Maple v Maple anonymity
Whether Article 29 of the Vienna Convention required a private Court of Appeal hearing
Relationship between FPR 2.66 chambers hearings and public law immunity claims
linked_authorities: Clibbery v Allen [2002] Fam 261
Pelling v Bruce-Williams (Secretary of State for Constitutional Affairs intervening) [2004] 2 FLR 823

notes: Sprung/Baird indemnity amendment ruling; appellate case management on pension mis-selling claim.

enrichment.short_title: Mandrake v Countrywide: amendment refused on Sprung but proceedings kept open for House of Lords
key_facts: Mandrake Holdings bought Mandrake Associates from Countrywide under a 1996 deed covenanting payment of pension mis-selling liabilities from the SIB review.

The claimants sought declaration that phase 2 liabilities were covered and, alternatively, rectification; in December 2004 they sought to amend to claim about £15.5m consequential loss from destruction of a turnaround sale strategy.
Lightman J refused permission to amend because Sprung v Royal Insurance bound him to hold that damages for late payment under a contract of indemnity were unavailable beyond discretionary interest.
Rix LJ dismissed the appeal on the law but exercised fresh discretion so the July 2005 trial on existing pleadings would not finally conclude proceedings pending possible House of Lords review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned permission to appeal treated as full appeal from refusal of permission to amend particulars of claim in pension indemnity proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal dismissed on the legal ground; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; trial on existing issues to proceed with new claim potentially revivable if the law changes.
enrichment.ratio: A first instance judge bound by Sprung must refuse an amendment seeking Hadley v Baxendale damages for breach of a contract of indemnity, but following Baird Textiles the court may manage proceedings so a merits trial proceeds while a point suitable for House of Lords review remains open without causing disproportionate hardship.
legal_issues: Whether damages are recoverable for late or non-payment under a contract of indemnity
Binding effect of Sprung v Royal Insurance on amendment applications
Case management discretion after strike-out or refusal of amendment under Baird Textiles
Prejudice from delay between January 2002 and December 2004 in raising the new claim
linked_authorities: Sprung v Royal Insurance [1999] 1 Lloyd's Rep IR 111
Baird Textile Holdings Ltd v Marks & Spencer plc [2001] 1 All ER 737
The Fanti [1991] 2 AC 1

enrichment.short_title: Murat v Special Commissioner: second appeal against same tax penalty decision dismissed
key_facts: Mr Murat appealed to Special Commissioner Wallace against HMRC penalty notices; penalties were reduced from £4,280 to £2,870.
He appealed to the High Court naming HMRC as respondent; Moses J dismissed the appeal on 24 October 2004 and Latham LJ refused permission to appeal on 6 April 2005.
Mr Murat then commenced fresh proceedings naming Commissioner Wallace as respondent in respect of the same December 2003 decision.
Ouseley J held the second proceedings were misconceived and an abuse of process because the successful party may support the tribunal decision on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to commence appeal proceedings against the Special Commissioner personally after prior unsuccessful appeal against HMRC.
enrichment.outcome: Proceedings dismissed as abuse of process; Mr Murat ordered to pay HMRC costs summarily assessed at £860.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant cannot pursue a second appeal against the same tribunal decision simply by naming a different respondent; points not raised on the first appeal cannot be relitigated, and the Special Commissioner is not an appropriate respondent where HMRC was the successful party.
legal_issues: Whether a second appeal naming the tribunal officer is permissible after failure against the revenue
Abuse of process and issue estoppel in tax penalty appeals
Article 8 challenge to requirement to disclose private drawings
Appropriateness of HMRC's costs

notes: Landmark Arkin litigation funder costs judgment; comprehensive Court of Appeal ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Arkin v Borchard: Arkin cap on professional litigation funder costs liability
key_facts: Impecunious claimant Mr Arkin pursued an unsuccessful Article 81/82 claim against shipping conference members with lawyers on CFAs and funding from MPC for expert evidence.
Defendants and Part 20 defendants sought section 51 costs orders against MPC exceeding £1.3 million; Colman J refused.
The Court of Appeal held professional funders who finance part of a claim for commercial reward should be liable for opposing costs only to the extent of funding provided.
MPC was ordered to pay £1.3 million by way of contribution; Borchard's Part 20 costs order was set aside and expert costs shared one-sixth among six conference parties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from Colman J's refusal to order costs against litigation funder MPC and from Part 20 costs allocation between shipping conference defendants.
enrichment.outcome: MPC appeal dismissed in part with £1.3 million costs contribution ordered; Borchard appeal on Part 20 costs allowed and costs reallocated among conference participants.
enrichment.ratio: Section 51 permits costs orders against non-party professional funders but justice requires capping their exposure at the amount of funding provided so access to justice is not destroyed; pure funders under Hamilton v Al Fayed remain protected, while funders controlling or benefiting as real parties may face wider liability.
legal_issues: Whether MPC should pay defendants' costs as a non-party funder
Distinction between pure funders and commercial litigation funders after Dymocks
Incidence of Part 20 costs between conference members after collective Article 81/82 defence
Whether champerty policy affects funder liability

notes: VAT fraud wrongful arrest and malicious prosecution appeal; full Court of Appeal review.

enrichment.short_title: Coudrat v HMRC: lawful arrest and prosecution in missing-trader mobile phone VAT fraud
key_facts: French national Vincent Coudrat was arrested with Luc Sommeyre at a London hotel on suspicion of VAT fraud linked to Tecniconsult Ltd's missing-trader mobile phone dealings.
He was charged under section 72(8) VATA, detained and later released when standing counsel advised insufficient evidence to continue.
The county court judge dismissed claims for wrongful arrest, false imprisonment and malicious prosecution.

The Court of Appeal upheld the judge on arrest, detention and prosecution, finding circumstantial evidence sufficient for reasonable suspicion and reasonable and probable cause despite Mr Rillie's doubts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Central London County Court dismissal of tort claims arising from VAT fraud investigation and prosecution.
enrichment.ratio: Reasonable suspicion of knowing involvement in Tecniconsult's VAT fraud was justified where the appellant was believed to be selling phones for the company; at charge stage prima facie circumstantial evidence of guilty knowledge under section 72(8) sufficed even if conviction prospects later looked weak, and malice cannot be inferred from an officer's mistaken assessment of evidence strength.
legal_issues: Whether Miss Crowson had reasonable grounds to suspect knowing involvement in VAT fraud
Lawfulness of continued detention under PACE section 37
Whether reasonable and probable cause existed to charge under section 72(8)
Whether prosecution continuation after counsel's oral advice evidenced malice

Glinski v McIver [1962] AC 726

enrichment.short_title: R v Bresa: unsafe section 34 direction where solicitor advice unexplained

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Adem Bresa was convicted at Lewes of wounding with intent after allegedly attacking Peter Smart with an iron bar over a former girlfriend.
At interview Bresa made no comment on solicitor's advice; at trial he relied on self-defence facts not mentioned in interview.

The judge directed the jury they had not heard why no-comment advice was given and that only the defendant could reveal privileged advice, without requiring sureness that silence was due to lack of a true explanation.
The Court of Appeal held the direction unfair under Condron, Chenia and Hoare; conviction quashed and retrial ordered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge; deportation recommendation adjourned pending retrial.
enrichment.ratio: A section 34 direction must strike a fair balance on legal professional privilege and require the jury to be sure the accused remained silent not because of advice but because he had no satisfactory explanation to give at interview; commenting that the defendant chose not to reveal advice without that safeguard renders a conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Proper form of section 34 direction where no-comment advice is unexplained
Dock identification of defendant by witness
Whether jury could infer fabrication of self-defence
Application of JSB specimen direction and Condron/ECHR standards
linked_authorities: R v Condron [1997] 1 WLR 827
R v Chenia [2003] 2 Cr App R 6
R v Hoare and Pierce [2004] EWCA Crim 784

enrichment.short_title: Re W (a child): appeal against refusal of adoption care plan for damaged toddler
key_facts: Lewisham sought a care order with adoption plan for CJ, a seriously traumatised toddler left with his aunt Sabrina after chaotic care by his mother Samantha.
Unanimous expert evidence from Dr Freedman, Dr Lucey and the guardian concluded Sabrina lacked long-term parenting capacity for CJ's therapeutic needs despite recent progress.
Judge Pearlman refused the care order and made interim residence and supervision orders in Sabrina's favour, but failed adequately to explain rejecting expert evidence.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside her order and remitted for review by Dr Lucey with provisional interim care order leaving CJ with Sabrina pending reassessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted after adjourned application concerning refusal of care order and adoption plan in care proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judge's order set aside; case remitted for further expert review and rehearing; interim care order in Lewisham's favour contemplated with CJ remaining with Sabrina pending review.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judge rejects strong unanimous expert and guardian evidence on parental capacity in public law proceedings she must give clear reasons addressing that evidence; failure to do so is fatal, though the court may remit rather than immediately substitute its own welfare decision in a finely balanced kinship case.
legal_issues: Whether Sabrina could meet CJ's long-term therapeutic and emotional needs
Adequacy of judicial reasons for departing from expert evidence
Balancing removal for adoption against stability with a blood relative
Inter-authority cooperation under section 27 Children Act

notes: Election petition judicial review; personal corruption finding quashed for procedural unfairness.

enrichment.short_title: Afzal v Election Court: quashing of personal corrupt practices finding in Aston ballot-rigging case
key_facts: Commissioner Mawrey QC found widespread postal vote fraud in Birmingham's Aston and Bordesley Green wards at the June 2004 council elections.
Muhammad Afzal was found personally guilty of corrupt practices for participating in ballot rigging at an NT warehouse on 8/9 June 2004, relying partly on WPC Grundy's identification.
Collins J refused permission to judicially review the personal finding; the Court of Appeal granted permission and heard the substantive claim.

The court quashed only the personal findings against Afzal because the Commissioner failed to ensure a fair opportunity to meet dock identification evidence and the suggestion Afzal passed himself off as Tariq Hussain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of permission to seek judicial review of Election Court findings that Mr Afzal was personally guilty of corrupt and illegal practices.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; personal corrupt practices findings against Mr Afzal quashed so he could vote in the pending parliamentary election; wider election voiding and findings against others untouched.
enrichment.ratio: An Election Court must afford a respondent a fair opportunity to deal with identification evidence and proposed adverse inferences; dock identification without recall of the witness or notice of a passing-off theory violates natural justice even in expedited election petition proceedings applying the criminal standard of proof.
legal_issues: Fairness of WPC Grundy's in-court identification of Mr Afzal
Conflict between identification evidence and police memorandum of names at the warehouse
Whether Mr Afzal was present during warehouse vote-rigging
Appropriate procedural protections where personal corrupt practices findings carry disfranchisement consequences

enrichment.short_title: OFT v Officers Club: misleading '70% off everything' reference pricing strategy
key_facts: The OFT sued Officers Club Ltd and director David Charlton over a long-running '70% off everything' strategy using short-lived 'Red Star' higher prices in a few stores before nationwide discounting.
TOC argued compliance with the DTI Price Indications Code and Article 10 ECHR commercial speech protection, citing years of trading without Part III prosecution.
The court held the notices implied goods had genuinely been offered at the higher reference price to ordinary consumers, which was not true of the artificial Red Star pricing model.
TOC's advertisements were misleading under the 1988 Regulations and a Community infringement under the Enterprise Act 2002; relief including injunction terms was deferred for a further hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited trial of liability under misleading advertisements regulations; injunction and final relief reserved.
enrichment.outcome: OFT succeeded on liability; further hearing directed to determine relief and form of order.
enrichment.ratio: Retail 'was/now' advertising that uses an artificially inflated reference price briefly offered in limited stores conveys to the ordinary consumer a misleading implied representation of a genuine higher price and significant sales at that price, notwithstanding Code compliance arguments and prior TSD tolerance.
legal_issues: Whether TOC's 70% off strategy was a misleading advertisement under Reg 2(2)
Effect of the Price Indications Code and Northumberland TSD cooperation
Article 10 ECHR challenge to enforcement under the Human Rights Act
Appropriateness and terms of an injunction under Reg 6(1)
linked_authorities: Casado Coca v Spain (1994) 18 EHRR 1
The Sunday Times v United Kingdom (1979) 2 EHRR 245
